title: Tanker Struck in Hormuz as Iran Names Strait the Core of US Talks
subhead: A Kuwait-flagged tanker was hit by a projectile inside the Strait of Hormuz and five Indian crew were rescued, while Tehran publicly framed control of the strait as the central issue in any deal to end the war, with the IEA now reporting over 80% of its record emergency release already delivered.

sections.heading: A Tanker Hit Inside Hormuz Tests the Fragile Flow Recovery
sections.body:
India's embassy in Oman said on Saturday that five Indian nationals aboard the Kuwait-flagged tanker MT Kazimah III were rescued after the vessel was 'struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz,' according to Anadolu Agency. The embassy thanked Omani authorities for coordinating the rescue, and India's external affairs ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said New Delhi remains committed to the safety of its seafarers.

The incident lands awkwardly for the market. Crude flows through Hormuz had been recovering through late September and into early October, which had pulled prices off their highs. Anadolu reported Friday that Brent had slipped to around $99.83 a barrel, down about 4.3% on the week, with WTI near $89.73, precisely because improved strait flows and expected emergency stock releases had eased supply fears. A fresh hit on a commercial tanker inside the strait shows how thin that recovery is.

OilPrice.com reported last week, citing Bloomberg, that three tankers had been attacked in the strait in a single week, prompting Indian refiners to change tactics and hire vessels rather than rely on producer-arranged shipping. Freight and insurance costs on Middle East routes have spiked since the February 28 US and Israeli strikes on Iran that opened the war.
sections.whyItMatters: The recovery in Hormuz traffic is being achieved under sustained attack, not because the threat has receded. Each tanker hit keeps the risk premium alive and keeps shipping costs elevated even when nominal volumes look normal.

sections.heading: Iran Says the Strait Is the Deal, Not the Nuclear File
sections.body:
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz is the main focus of Iran's negotiations to end the war with the US, according to Anadolu Agency citing the state-run IRNA news agency. 'Securing the Strait of Hormuz, or restoring security to this waterway, requires specific steps from the American side,' Baqaei said, listing an end to interference with Iranian commercial shipping, an end to sanctions, and other measures.

Notably, Baqaei said Iran's top leadership has not discussed allowing IAEA inspectors to return, and that the latest US proposal was almost identical to earlier ones, with Washington still focused on the nuclear file. That is a meaningful inversion: Tehran is signalling that it wants the conversation to be about maritime access and sanctions relief, while Washington keeps returning to enrichment and inspections.

Efforts to end the war have run since a June framework deal intended to cover navigation through the strait and Iran's nuclear program. Qatari-mediated talks in New York recently broke down — US Secretary of State Marco Rubio asked an Iranian delegation including Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to leave, while Iran's UN mission denied it was forced out, per Anadolu.
sections.whyItMatters: The two sides are not negotiating the same agenda. Iran is pricing its reopening of Hormuz against sanctions relief and an end to the naval blockade of its ports; the US keeps anchoring on the nuclear file. That mismatch is why the talks keep stalling.

sections.heading: IEA Says 80% of Record Emergency Release Is Already Out
sections.body:
IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol told G7 leaders on Friday that around 325 million barrels of the 400 million barrels pledged in the agency's March 11 collective action have already been released — more than 80% of the largest coordinated release in the agency's history, according to Anadolu Agency. Birol said markets remain under significant pressure, particularly in diesel, and that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries are adding to the squeeze.

On Friday the G7 agreed to release a further 100 million barrels of oil and fuel over four months, with a substantial share of the diesel frontloaded into the first 20 days. The group also agreed to coordinate refinery maintenance and to refrain from imposing energy export restrictions on each other — a direct nod to US pressure over a possible diesel export ban. G7 leaders asked the IEA to report on implementation within 20 days.

The numbers matter because they show how much of the strategic cushion has already been spent. A large fraction of the first tranche is gone, and the new 100-million-barrel tranche is smaller and slower.
sections.whyItMatters: Emergency reserves are a finite tool, and the first and largest tranche is nearly exhausted. The follow-on release is smaller, which limits how much further price suppression governments can buy if the strait deteriorates.

sections.heading: Canada Fast-Tracks a 1-Million-bpd Pacific Pipeline to Asia
sections.body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Ottawa will list a proposed 1 million-barrel-per-day oil pipeline to the Pacific coast as a project of national interest, sending it through a single federal review that Ottawa aims to complete by September 1, 2027, OilPrice.com reported. The line would run from Alberta to southern British Columbia, largely following the existing Trans Mountain corridor, led by Trans Mountain Corp. and Pembina Pipeline, with federal and Alberta governments expected to hold a majority stake and Indigenous communities offered at least 10% ownership.

Alberta estimates construction at C$35.2 billion to C$43.7 billion; Ottawa projects more than C$20 billion in annual GDP and up to 140,000 jobs at peak. Canada still sends more than 90% of its crude exports to the US, and its only Pacific escape route, the 890,000-bpd Trans Mountain line, is already running at capacity. Notably, China has become the largest buyer of Trans Mountain's seaborne exports at roughly 60% of shipments, per the Canadian government — barrels that never have to clear Hormuz.

Ottawa and Alberta are also pursuing another 300,000 to 400,000 bpd of capacity on the existing Trans Mountain system. The new line still needs a final route, approvals and consultation with British Columbia and Indigenous communities.
sections.whyItMatters: The Hormuz crisis has made non-Gulf barrels structurally more valuable to Asia. Canada is now moving to convert that demand into a permanent outlet that bypasses both the strait and US market dependence.

sections.heading: Asia's Import-Dependent Economies Are Paying the Most
sections.body:
Taiwan is allocating the equivalent of $13 billion in energy cost support for state utility Taipower and refiner CPC, Reuters reported via OilPrice.com, to offset cost inflation from the Middle East war. Taiwan relies on imports for 94% to 97% of its consumption and is heavily dependent on LNG sourced from Qatar and the UAE. Its economy ministry warned that without supplementary budgets, CPC and Taipower 'may struggle to continue serving as price stabilisers.' Natural gas supplies over 23% of the island's power, oil almost 36% and coal nearly 32%, and TSMC alone consumes as much as 8% of national electricity.

Pakistan is weighing allowing power plants and private firms to import LNG directly on the spot market, a source told Bloomberg, as the country struggles with an energy crisis since the Iran war disrupted Qatar's term supplies. Pakistan's Energy Ministry has proposed easing regulations that currently keep spot procurement largely with state-owned Pakistan LNG Ltd. Qatar has now extended its LNG force majeure to Asia and Europe by another month, through the end of November, as Qatari cargoes remain largely blocked at Hormuz.

Türkiye is also feeling the squeeze: Anadolu reported the country's energy import bill rose 33.8% year-on-year in August to $6.46 billion, accounting for 22.5% of total imports.
sections.whyItMatters: The war's cost is falling hardest on import-dependent Asian and emerging economies that cannot substitute supply quickly. These are fiscal and political pressures building well beyond the Gulf, and they are the constituencies with the least cushion.

sections.heading: Europe Bets on Grids and Storage as the Strait Shock Lingers
sections.body:
Investment in EU and Norwegian electricity distribution grids could reach €48 billion by 2027, according to Eurelectric's 'Power Barometer 2026' report cited by Anadolu Agency, up from €36 billion in 2024 and €24 billion in 2021 — an average annual growth of 12.5%, nearly doubling over six years. Eurelectric flagged permitting delays, slow cost recovery, regulatory uncertainty, supply-chain bottlenecks and skilled-worker shortages as risks to the rollout.

The connection-queue problem is stark: Italy has 348 GW of variable renewable projects awaiting grid connection, close to six times its installed capacity, while Germany has around 480 GW of battery storage connection requests and Italy 277 GW. Operational utility-scale battery storage in the EU more than doubled in 2025, reaching 11.2 GW in early 2026, led by Germany at 2.9 GW.

Separately, the UN warned that global fuel subsidies amid the oil price shock could top $1 trillion this year, as reported via OilPrice.com — a figure that undercuts the fiscal room many governments need for grid and transition spending.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe is using the strait shock to justify accelerating electrification and grid buildout, but the queue numbers show the bottleneck is permitting and grid capacity, not ambition. The subsidy burden competing with that investment is the hard constraint.

bottomLine: The weekend's clearest signal is that Hormuz remains contested even as flows nominally recover: a Kuwait-flagged tanker was hit by a projectile inside the strait and five Indian crew had to be rescued, following three attacks in a single week. Iran, meanwhile, has reframed the negotiation as being about the strait and sanctions relief rather than the nuclear file, while the US keeps returning to enrichment. On supply, the IEA has already delivered over 80% of its record 400-million-barrel release, and the new 100-million-barrel G7 tranche is smaller and slower — the emergency cushion is thinning. The structural response is visible in Canada's fast-tracked 1-million-bpd Pacific pipeline aimed at Asian buyers who no longer want Gulf barrels, and in Asian importers like Taiwan ($13 billion) and Pakistan scrambling to absorb costs. The war's price is being paid most heavily outside the Gulf, by economies that cannot reroute supply quickly.
sources: Anadolu Agency, OilPrice.com, Bloomberg (via OilPrice.com), Reuters (via OilPrice.com), International Energy Agency, Eurelectric, IRNA (via Anadolu Agency), UK Maritime Trade Operations (via OilPrice.com), United Nations (via OilPrice.com)
